title: Choosing a Futures Tick Database: Test Event Fidelity Before Query Speed
author: wang vball
summary: Which database is best for futures tick data? Choose one that preserves the events your application needs before comparing query speed. Two trades can share a timestamp, continuous symbols can change their underlying contracts, and database deduplication rules differ. A small synthetic replay test can expose these mistakes before a fast query turns them into plausible but incorrect results. For trade analytics, start with a trustworthy trade-event archive and a database whose duplicate and correction handling you can verify. For order-book reconstruction, trade records alone are insufficient: you also need the relevant book events and recovery rules. A fast database cannot reconstruct events that its upstream feed never supplied. This is an evaluation method, not a database speed ranking or a claim that one market-data service covers every futures venue. Separate the feed from the database A market-data API delivers a documented representation of the market. A raw event log preserves what your collector received. A query database organizes that material for analysis. These responsibilities can share infrastructure, but they should have separate acceptance criteria. TickDB is a useful example of the first layer. Its current documentation describes REST and WebSocket trade data for China and Hong Kong futures. That establishes a documented data-source option for those markets; it does not establish a user-queryable SQL database, exchange-native packet capture, or complete historical replay. Preserve the original message, source, receive time and a durable collector receipt identifier before normalization. Keep source event time separately, with its documented unit and meaning. Receipt order can reproduce what your collector observed; sorting by event time answers a different question. Neither ordering should silently replace the other. Suggested architecture: delivery, preservation and analytical queries are separate responsibilities, not a vendor architecture diagram. Decide what identifies a futures event A symbol plus a millisecond timestamp is not a universal event key. Two genuine trades can arrive with the same timestamp and price. Collapsing them can undercount volume while leaving a chart looking reasonable. Use a documented event identifier within its documented scope when one exists. That scope may require a source, venue, session and instrument. Do not assume an ID is globally unique or survives a session reset. If the source provides no reliable identifier, preserve separate receipts and mark identity unresolved instead of silently deleting apparent duplicates. The distinction matters when adapting TickDB messages. Its WebSocket documentation specifies single-trade objects for China and Hong Kong futures, and explicitly lists a trade ID for Hong Kong futures. The China futures example does not establish the same identifier guarantee. One universal adapter that assumes every message has an ID would overstate the documented contract. Two events can share a timestamp. This synthetic example illustrates identity, not measured exchange traffic. Contract identity needs the same care. Store the concrete contract and the effective mapping of any continuous alias separately. TickDB's data specification distinguishes regular China futures contracts from continuous symbols intended for market tracking, not delivery. Do not treat a continuous series as one permanent tradable contract. Record the roll rule and any price adjustment before comparing results across a rollover. Test the projection without destroying the evidence Keep the raw deliveries immutable and build a separate analytical projection. The following standard-library Python example uses a deliberately synthetic schema. It assumes source-defined IDs scoped by source, session and contract, plus explicitly ordered revision numbers. Those are test assumptions, not fields promised by every provider. The seven deliveries include two trades at the same time, a repeated delivery, a correction, a late older revision and two receipts without IDs. The projection retains both identified trades, applies the correction, and leaves the unidentified receipts unresolved. def project ( events ) : """Synthetic schema: IDs and revision order are source-defined.""" latest , unresolved = { } , [ ] for event in events : row = dict ( event ) if row . get ( "event_id" ) is None : unresolved . append ( row ) # Never guess identity from time/price. continue key = tuple ( row [ k ] for k in ( "source" , "session" , "contract" , "event_id" ) ) old = latest . get ( key ) if old is None or row [ "revision" ] > old [ "revision" ] : latest [ key ] = row elif row [ "revision" ] == old [ "revision" ] : payload = lambda r : { k : v for k , v in r . items ( ) if k != "receipt_id" } if payload ( row ) != payload ( old ) : raise ValueError ( "Conflicting payload at the same revision" ) return list ( latest . values ( ) ) , unresolved def example ( ) : base = dict ( source = "synthetic" , session = "S1" , contract = "FUT-A" , event_ms = 1000 , price = "100.00" , revision = 1 ) a = dict ( base , event_id = "A" , receipt_id = 1 ) b = dict ( base , event_id = "B" , receipt_id = 2 ) deliveries = [ a , b , dict ( a , receipt_id = 3 ) , dict ( a , revision = 2 , price = "100.25" , receipt_id = 4 ) , dict ( a , receipt_id = 5 ) , dict ( base , event_id = None , receipt_id = 6 ) , dict ( base , event_id = None , receipt_id = 7 ) ] resolved , unresolved = project ( deliveries ) assert len ( resolved ) == 2 and len ( unresolved ) == 2 assert next ( r for r in resolved if r [ "event_id" ] == "A" ) [ "price" ] == "100.25" print ( "7 deliveries: 2 resolved events, 2 unresolved receipts" ) if __name__ == "__main__" : example ( ) The local synthetic run prints 7 deliveries: 2 resolved events, 2 unresolved receipts . It does not prove market completeness, throughput or database durability. The unresolved receipts may include duplicates; retaining them avoids making an unsupported identity decision. Do not aggregate them as confirmed distinct trades without further reconciliation. A changed payload at the same revision raises an error rather than silently picking a winner. Production ingestion should quarantine that conflict while retaining its raw message. This example does not implement cancellations, persistent checkpoints or a source-specific sequence protocol. Add those cases according to the feed contract, including sequence resets and recovery after a collector restart. Compare duplicate semantics before performance QuestDB and ClickHouse illustrate why “supports deduplication” is not a sufficient selection criterion. QuestDB's current deduplication documentation describes explicit key columns, including the designated timestamp, for WAL tables. Its UPSERT mode keeps the latest write for matching keys. That is write order, not necessarily the highest source revision: a late old correction needs deliberate handling. Enabling deduplication also does not clean up pre-existing duplicates retroactively. ClickHouse ReplacingMergeTree identifies duplicates through the sorting key and removes them during background merges whose timing is not guaranteed. A query cannot assume those merges have already completed. Evaluate query-time replacement semantics, including FINAL where appropriate, and measure the actual query shape you will use. Neither behavior is inherently the right answer for every workload. An immutable audit archive and a latest-corrected analytical view have different requirements. Feed the same test deliveries into each candidate and compare the results immediately after ingestion, after maintenance, and after replay. Check contract separation, retained revisions and unresolved records, not just the final row count. Benchmark only the candidates that preserve meaning Once the semantic tests pass, measure your real workload: sustained ingestion, late arrivals, narrow contract-and-time queries, broader aggregates, and recovery. Hold the input dataset, hardware, retention policy and query results constant. Report cold and warm query behavior, concurrency and storage usage rather than publishing a single unexplained latency number. Validate backfill separately. TickDB's documented REST trades endpoint accepts a symbol and a limit of up to 1,000 records; that alone does not demonstrate arbitrary time-range recovery or lossless polling. Ask what can be recovered after a longer outage, and test the exact boundary. Storage and redistribution rights also need separate confirmation. Choose the simplest system that passes these checks at your required scale. If a candidate cannot explain which events survived replay, a faster query is answering an uncertain question. Documentation checked November 14, 2026: TickDB Data Specification and Trade documentation; QuestDB Deduplication; ClickHouse ReplacingMergeTree. Code results are synthetic local validation, not a provider benchmark.

title: Building a Name Numerology Calculator in Python: Chaldean vs Pythagorean, With Tests
author: NumsExpert
summary: Name numerology turns the letters of a name into numbers. Two letter-value systems dominate: Pythagorean (1–9 repeating) and Chaldean (1–8, based on sound vibration). The same name gives different totals under each system, which is exactly what makes this a good small calculator project — the rules are simple, the edge cases are real, and the arithmetic is easy to test. This post builds a dependency-free Python calculator for the three classic numbers — Destiny (all letters), Soul Urge (vowels only), Personality (consonants only) — and tests it against hand-checked examples. The letter tables PYTHAGOREAN = { "A" : 1 , "B" : 2 , "C" : 3 , "D" : 4 , "E" : 5 , "F" : 6 , "G" : 7 , "H" : 8 , "I" : 9 , "J" : 1 , "K" : 2 , "L" : 3 , "M" : 4 , "N" : 5 , "O" : 6 , "P" : 7 , "Q" : 8 , "R" : 9 , "S" : 1 , "T" : 2 , "U" : 3 , "V" : 4 , "W" : 5 , "X" : 6 , "Y" : 7 , "Z" : 8 , } CHALDEAN = { "A" : 1 , "B" : 2 , "C" : 3 , "D" : 4 , "E" : 5 , "F" : 8 , "G" : 3 , "H" : 5 , "I" : 1 , "J" : 1 , "K" : 2 , "L" : 3 , "M" : 4 , "N" : 5 , "O" : 7 , "P" : 8 , "Q" : 1 , "R" : 2 , "S" : 3 , "T" : 4 , "U" : 6 , "V" : 6 , "W" : 6 , "X" : 5 , "Y" : 1 , "Z" : 7 , } Reduction and master numbers Totals reduce to a single digit by summing digits — except master numbers 11, 22 and 33, which standard practice keeps as-is: MASTER_NUMBERS = ( 11 , 22 , 33 ) def reduce_number ( total , keep_masters = True ) : while total > 9 : if keep_masters and total in MASTER_NUMBERS : return total total = sum ( int ( digit ) for digit in str ( total ) ) return total The letter Y The fiddly edge case. The most common textbook rule: Y counts as a vowel only when a word has no other vowel (A, E, I, O, U); otherwise it is a consonant. So in "LYN", Y is the vowel; in "MARY", A is the vowel and Y is a consonant. State the rule explicitly in your code — different traditions differ, and silent assumptions are how calculators disagree. Putting it together VOWELS = set ( "AEIOU" ) def calculate ( name , system = "pythagorean" ) : table = { "pythagorean" : PYTHAGOREAN , "chaldean" : CHALDEAN } [ system ] destiny = soul = personality = 0 for word in name . upper ( ) . split ( ) : letters = [ ch for ch in word if ch . isalpha ( ) ] for letter in letters : value = table [ letter ] destiny += value is_vowel = letter in VOWELS or ( letter == "Y" and not any ( ch in VOWELS for ch in letters ) ) if is_vowel : soul += value else : personality += value return ( reduce_number ( destiny ) , reduce_number ( soul ) , reduce_number ( personality ) , ) Verified example: MICHAEL Hand-checked, and covered by the test suite: System Destiny Soul Urge Personality Pythagorean 33 (total 33) 6 (total 15) 9 (total 18) Chaldean 22 (total 22) 7 (total 7) 6 (total 15) Pythagorean: M4 + I9 + C3 + H8 + A1 + E5 + L3 = 33, a master number, so it stays 33. Chaldean: M4 + I1 + C3 + H5 + A1 + E5 + L3 = 22, also kept. Same name, different systems, different answers — which is why any calculator must say which system it used. Tests worth writing At minimum: master-number preservation (11/22/33 kept, 38 → 11 kept), the MICHAEL totals above in both systems, the Y rule in both directions ("LYN" vs "MARY"), and case/whitespace handling. If those pass, the calculator agrees with hand calculation on every name I checked. If you want to check your own addition without running code, the free calculator at namenumerologycal.com runs both systems side by side. Name numerology is a reflection tool from a symbolic tradition, not a prediction or a diagnosis — the code just does the arithmetic honestly.

title: Deploy a Telegram bot for free with Claude Code
author: Philipp Shayzhanov
summary: You want a Telegram bot that works all the time, not only when your laptop is on. For that you need three things: a bot token from BotFather, a public HTTPS address, so Telegram can send messages to your bot, a server that keeps the bot running. The token is easy. The other two usually mean a VPS: you rent a server, set up a web server, get a certificate, and make sure the bot restarts when it crashes. This guide skips all of that. You tell Claude Code what bot you want. It builds the bot on vbtnl and gives you a live address. The full code is below, so you can see what runs. you Claude Code vbtnl Telegram | | | | | "build a bot" | | | |--------------------->| write, run, publish | | | |--------------------->| setWebhook (HTTPS) | | | |--------------------->| | | | | | a message to the bot | |-------------------------------------------------------------------->| | | | POST /webhook | | | |<---------------------| | | | sendMessage | | | |--------------------->| | the bot replies | |<--------------------------------------------------------------------| What you need Claude Code. Codex works too, the steps are the same. A Telegram account. A vbtnl account. The free plan is enough for one bot, and you don't need a card. Step 1. Get a token from BotFather In Telegram, open @BotFather and send /newbot . Choose a name, then a username that ends with bot . BotFather sends you a token. It looks like 123456789:AAH... . Don't share the token. Anyone who has it can control your bot. Step 2. Connect vbtnl to Claude Code vbtnl is an MCP server. You add it to Claude Code once: claude mcp add --transport http vbtnl https://api.vbtnl.com/mcp Then type /mcp in Claude Code, pick vbtnl and log in. Now Claude Code can create projects on vbtnl, write files there, run commands and publish. Step 3. Ask for the bot Here is the prompt: Build a Telegram bot on vbtnl. It answers /start with a greeting and repeats any other message back. Use a webhook, not polling. I will give you the bot token as a secret. Claude Code will ask for the token. Paste it in the chat. It saves the token as a secret, so the token never ends up in a file. Then the agent does the work, step by step: create_project creates a project with two addresses: a draft for testing and production for real use. set_secrets saves the token and a random WEBHOOK_SECRET . write_files writes the code. exec sends a test message to the draft to check that it answers. publish puts the bot into production. The code The agent writes the code for you, so your bot will look a bit different. But it will be close to this. There are three files. vbtnl.json tells vbtnl how to start the app: { "stack" : "python" , "start" : "uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port $PORT" } requirements.txt : fastapi uvicorn httpx main.py : import os from contextlib import asynccontextmanager import httpx from fastapi import FastAPI , Header , HTTPException , Request TOKEN = os . environ [ "TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN" ] SECRET = os . environ [ "WEBHOOK_SECRET" ] API = f "https://api.telegram.org/bot{TOKEN}" @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan ( app : FastAPI ) : # Only production connects to Telegram. The draft is tested with curl. if os . environ . get ( "VBTNL_ENV" ) == "prod" : async with httpx . AsyncClient ( ) as client : await client . post ( f "{API}/setWebhook" , json = { "url" : f "{os.environ['VBTNL_URL']}/webhook" , "secret_token" : SECRET , } ) yield app = FastAPI ( lifespan = lifespan ) @app . post ( "/webhook" ) async def webhook ( request : Request , x_telegram_bot_api_secret_token : str = Header ( default = "" ) ) : if x_telegram_bot_api_secret_token != SECRET : raise HTTPException ( status_code = 403 ) update = await request . json ( ) message = update . get ( "message" ) or { } chat_id = ( message . get ( "chat" ) or { } ) . get ( "id" ) if chat_id is None : return { "ok" : True } text = message . get ( "text" , "" ) if text == "/start" : reply = "Hi! Send me anything and I will repeat it." else : reply = f "You said: {text}" async with httpx . AsyncClient ( ) as client : await client . post ( f "{API}/sendMessage" , json = { "chat_id" : chat_id , "text" : reply } ) return { "ok" : True } You don't set PORT , VBTNL_ENV or VBTNL_URL yourself, vbtnl does it. VBTNL_URL is the public address of the bot. When the bot starts, it sends this address to Telegram, so you never copy a URL by hand. Webhook or polling? A bot can get messages in two ways: Polling. The bot asks Telegram again and again: "Any new messages?" Webhook. Telegram sends every new message to the bot's address. Polling is fine on your laptop. On a server, a webhook is better. The bot does nothing until a message comes, it answers faster, and it is just a normal web app. Telegram sends webhooks only to HTTPS addresses. Every vbtnl address already has HTTPS, so there is no certificate to set up. Watch out. One bot token can have only one webhook. If both the draft and production register it, the one that started last gets the messages and the other one is silent. That is why the code registers the webhook only in production. The secret token The webhook address is public. Anyone who finds it can send fake messages to your bot. Telegram has a simple fix. When you call setWebhook , you also send a secret_token . Then Telegram puts this value in the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header of every request. The code checks the header and answers 403 if it is wrong. Keep this secret where you keep the bot token: in the project secrets, not in the code. Step 4. Test, then publish The draft doesn't get real messages from Telegram. So ask the agent to test it: Send a fake /start update to the draft and show me the response. It sends a fake message with curl and shows you the answer and the logs. If everything looks good, write: Ship it. The agent publishes the bot. Production starts, connects to Telegram, and the bot is live. Open it in Telegram and send /start . Make the bot write first Sometimes you want the bot to send something on its own. For example: Every day at 9:00 UTC send "Good morning" to my chat. My chat id is 123456789. The agent adds a small script and a schedule to vbtnl.json : { "stack" : "python" , "start" : "uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port $PORT" , "cron" : [ { "schedule" : "0 9 * * *" , "run" : "python daily.py" } ] } Schedules use the normal cron format and UTC time. A project can have up to 10 of them. Don't know your chat id? Send any message to the bot and ask the agent to find it in the logs. If something goes wrong The bot doesn't answer after publishing. Ask the agent to check the production logs and the webhook. Most of the time the token is wrong. It worked, but stopped after a change. Ask the agent to roll back. Every publish is saved as a version, and going back takes one step. You want to save users or messages. Ask for a database. The agent adds Postgres, and the bot gets its address in DATABASE_URL . Don't save data to files in production: files are lost when the app restarts. Is it really free and online 24/7? For one bot, yes. The free plan has one project, and you don't need a card. Production doesn't sleep when nobody writes to the bot. This is important for bots. Many free hosts stop your app after a few minutes without traffic. With a webhook that breaks the bot: Telegram sends a message, and nothing is there to answer. On vbtnl only the draft sleeps, and it wakes up when the agent works with it. On the free plan the bot gets 0.5 vCPU, 1.25 GB of RAM, a 1 GB Postgres database and an address on vbtnl.site . What it costs One bot is free. Paid plans start at $19 a month. You get more projects, more CPU and memory, and your own domain. See pricing . Questions Do I need a VPS for a Telegram bot? No. With a VPS you install Python, a web server, a certificate and a process manager yourself. Here vbtnl runs the app, gives it HTTPS and restarts it when needed. The agent does the setup. Can I use Codex instead of Claude Code? Yes. Add vbtnl with codex mcp add vbtnl --url https://api.vbtnl.com/mcp , then run codex mcp login vbtnl . Use the same prompt. Can I write the bot in Node.js? Yes. vbtnl runs Python 3.12 and Node.js 22. Say which one you want in the prompt. Do I need to know Python? No. The agent writes the code and fixes it. The code is here so you can see what runs, not because you need to type it. I already have a bot. Can I move it here? Yes. Ask the agent to put your files into a project and publish them. Two rules: the app must listen on $PORT , and it must read the token from an environment variable. More answers are in the FAQ . Build your bot with one message. Connect vbtnl to Claude Code or Codex, describe the bot, and get a live address. Originally published on the vbtnl blog .

title: CoStar Alternative for Public Commercial Real Estate Listings
author: KinderBB
summary: If you need public on-market commercial real estate listings in a spreadsheet or API, KazKN's LoopNet + Crexi Scraper is a practical CoStar alternative. It searches both platforms, merges the results, removes cross-platform duplicates, and normalizes price, size, and cap rate for $18 per 1,000 results. It is not a replacement for CoStar's full enterprise and private-data feature set; it is for brokers, acquisition teams, and analysts who need exportable public listings. When this CoStar alternative fits The best fit is a team that repeatedly rebuilds a market spreadsheet from public listings. A small broker might need current asking prices and broker details for one city. An acquisition analyst might need building size, NOI, cap rate, and days on market for a weekly review. In those cases, paying for each returned listing can be a better match than buying a broad enterprise system. The tool covers public on-market inventory from LoopNet and Crexi, not private or off-market ownership data. What you need Reasonable choice Public LoopNet and Crexi listings in one file LoopNet + Crexi Scraper CoStar's broader enterprise and private-data features CoStar is the closer fit A few listings checked once Manual collection may be enough A custom pipeline controlled by your developers A DIY script, with its maintenance work This is deliberately not a like-for-like comparison. The question is whether your workflow needs public listing rows or a wider enterprise data product. Your options: manual collection, DIY, or a hosted tool Collect listings by hand Manual collection means running searches on each site, copying the listings, and reconciling properties that appear twice. It gives you direct control over every row and can work for a very small, occasional search. The recurring work is the drawback: two searches, two layouts, duplicate properties, and inconsistent price, size, and cap-rate formats. Write your own commercial real estate data scraper A DIY script gives your team control over collection, storage, and transformations. You also own the operational work: source changes, access restrictions, retries, field normalization, deduplication, and monitoring. You must separately review each site's terms and decide which requests and uses are permitted. This route makes sense when custom requirements justify maintaining the pipeline. A script that only copies pages still does not solve the spreadsheet problem unless it also produces consistent, comparable rows. Use a hosted, pay-per-result tool The hosted option runs the collection and normalization for you. This actor searches LoopNet and Crexi, selects the most complete record when it identifies a cross-platform match, and marks the other platform in also_listed_on . Results go to an Apify dataset that you can export as CSV, Excel, or JSON, or retrieve through an API. Is there an official API? I could not confirm a public official CoStar API for this exact public-listing export workflow from the sources reviewed. The actor also does not claim to be an official LoopNet or Crexi API. It is a scraper hosted on Apify, and the API described below starts that actor and reads its output dataset. That distinction matters when searching for a commercial real estate listings API: API access to scraper output is not the same as an API provided or endorsed by the listing site. Run the LoopNet + Crexi Scraper step by step Open the LoopNet + Crexi Scraper tool page and open the actor on Apify. For a manual US search, enter a state and, optionally, a city or county. The example below uses Dallas, Texas. Choose LoopNet, Crexi, or both. Manual mode uses both sources by default. Sale listings are the default transaction type; filters for asset class, price, cap rate, and building size are also available. Set maxResultsPerSource . The value is a maximum target for each selected source, not a guaranteed final row count. Keep deduplicate enabled to merge likely cross-platform matches. It defaults to true . Decide whether you need optional listing-detail enrichment for public broker contacts and richer details. It is disabled by default and billed separately when enabled and actually applied to a row. Start the run, review its status and returned rows, then export the dataset or read it through the API. A smaller result set can reflect limited qualifying inventory, rows removed by filters, or cross-platform deduplication. Check the run summary rather than treating the requested maximum as a delivery promise. Reuse an existing LoopNet or Crexi search You can supply official LoopNet or Crexi search or listing URLs through startUrls instead of using manual fields. Supported URLs take priority: they determine the source and search criteria, and manual fields are ignored. URL mode is capped at 200 results per source. Some advanced source filters cannot be reproduced exactly, so review the run status for partial results and confirm that the returned listings still match your intent. Call the commercial real estate listings API with Python Install the official Apify Python client and set an Apify API token in your environment: python -m pip install apify-client export APIFY_TOKEN = "your_apify_token" This example uses the actor's real Dallas input and waits for the run before reading the default dataset: import os from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ "APIFY_TOKEN" ] ) run_input = { "city" : "Dallas" , "state" : "TX" , "maxResultsPerSource" : 100 , } run = client . actor ( "kazkn/commercial-real-estate-brokerage-intel" ) . call ( run_input = run_input ) items = client . dataset ( run [ "defaultDatasetId" ] ) . list_items ( ) . items for item in items : print ( item . get ( "listing_url" ) , item . get ( "asking_price_or_rent" ) ) The explicit input avoids relying on console prefills. Because sourcesEnabled and transactionTypes are omitted, the documented defaults apply: both sources and sale listings. The returned items are Python dictionaries ready for your own CSV process, database loader, or analysis code. Output fields and a real example row The dataset keeps the source link alongside normalized property and financial fields. Availability still depends on what each public listing declares. Field What it contains source loopnet or crexi listing_url Link to the public listing also_listed_on The other platform when the property appears on both market City and state of the search address Full street address asset_class Office, retail, industrial, multifamily, and more sub_type Finer property type, such as loft or creative space building_size_sqft Building size in square feet asking_price_or_rent Asking price or rent as shown by the source noi Net operating income when the listing declares it cap_rate Listed cap rate, or one computed from declared NOI and price price_per_sqft Price per square foot days_on_market Days on market when the source shows it broker_name Listing broker, when public broker_company Brokerage firm broker_phone Public phone, or marked as not publicly discoverable Here is a masked real output row: { "address" : "Richardson, TX 75080" , "asking_price_or_rent" : "$3,250,000" , "city" : "Richardson" , "building_size_sqft" : "226,723" , "source" : "loopnet" , "state" : "TX" , "zip" : "75080" , "market" : "Richardson, TX" , "transaction_type" : "sale" , "asking_amount_usd" : "3,250,000" } For cap rates, the actor passes through a source-listed value or calculates NOI divided by asking price when both are declared. It does not expose a model-only estimate as a fact. Verify source values before underwriting or making an investment decision. What a run costs The result price is $18 per 1,000 results , which is $0.018 per returned unique listing . Cross-platform duplicates are merged rather than delivered as separate primary rows. Returned unique listings Result charges 100 $1.80 250 $4.50 1,000 $18.00 The README also lists a $0.06 actor-start charge on the Apify Free plan. At that plan's $18 per 1,000 result rate, a run returning 100 unique listings costs $1.80 in result charges plus $0.06 to start, or $1.86 before optional enrichment or monitoring charges . Prices can vary by Apify plan. With the Dallas example, maxResultsPerSource: 100 does not mean you will receive or pay for exactly 200 rows. Available inventory, explicit filters, and duplicate removal affect the final count. Optional listing-detail enrichment is a separate per-enriched-row event, so leave it off when you only need the base listing export. What are the rules? Public commercial real estate data can still be protected by contractual terms and applicable law. Public access does not automatically grant permission for automated collection, redistribution, or every commercial use. Review the current LoopNet and Crexi terms, comply with access controls, and assess your intended use. Do not treat a technical ability to retrieve a page as legal permission. Broker names, companies, phone numbers, and other contact details can be personal data even when published for business purposes. If GDPR applies to your processing, identify a lawful basis, collect only what you need, define retention, secure the data, and handle applicable individual rights. Keep the source URL so your team can review provenance and check corrections or removal requests. This article is general information, not legal advice. Ask a qualified lawyer about your sources, locations, and use case, especially before large-scale redistribution or outreach. FAQ Is this a complete CoStar replacement? No. It is a CoStar alternative for public on-market listing collection and export. Teams needing CoStar's full enterprise and private-data feature set should not expect this actor to replace it. Is this an official CoStar, LoopNet, or Crexi API? No. It is an Apify-hosted scraper with API access to runs and datasets. No. Its stated scope is public listings from LoopNet and Crexi. It is designed for market scans, acquisition lists, broker-lead review, and repeatable exports of that public inventory. title: How to Scrape Funda Property Listings in Python with Funda Scraper
author: ReventaData
summary: By the end of this tutorial you will have a Python script that pulls Dutch homes for sale or for rent from funda.nl into structured rows: asking price, address, living area, rooms, bedrooms, energy label, agency and photo links. Funda is a Dutch property portal, and its search pages are not friendly to a quick requests script. In my tests on 7 November 2026, plain HTTP clients got an "Access Denied" stub or a verification page instead of results. Funda Scraper ( reventadata/funda-scraper ) is the Apify Actor I built to deal with that. You send it a search, it returns one row per listing. This guide runs it from Python with the Apify API client, and the sample rows below come from a real capture of a Utrecht rental search, not from an invented example. Prerequisites You need three things: Python 3.11 or newer (the Apify client for Python 3.x requires it). A free Apify account , which you can create with an email address or a GitHub login. Your API token , from Settings > API & Integrations in Apify Console. Install the client and export the token: pip install -U "apify-client~=3.0" export APIFY_API_TOKEN = "your_apify_token_here" No scraping code is needed on your side. The Actor does the fetching. What you'll achieve You will search funda.nl for rentals in Utrecht up to 1,500 EUR per month, read the rows in Python and print a one-line summary per listing, including a price per square metre that you work out yourself from two fields. Funda lists more than homes, so a rental search also returns parking spaces and storage units. You will see how to spot them and how to filter them out. The same script works for a buyer comparing asking prices across towns, a tenant watching new rentals, or an analyst building a table of energy labels by neighbourhood. Only the input changes. Step 1: Open Funda Scraper Open the Funda Scraper page on Apify Store . The Try for free button there opens the Actor in Apify Console. This tutorial uses the API from Python, so you only need the Actor name, reventadata/funda-scraper . Step 2: Choose the search The search is described by a handful of input fields: offering : sale or rent . Anything else is refused before the run starts. areas : a list of Funda area slugs such as amsterdam or utrecht , copied from the selected_area part of a funda.nl search URL. Each area is one search, and a listing found twice is kept once. Leave the list empty and the Actor searches the whole Netherlands. objectType : empty (every type), house or apartment . sort : relevance (Funda's default) or newest . maxPrice and minPrice : in EUR, and for rentals per month. minLivingAreaM2 , maxLivingAreaM2 , minBedrooms : size filters. maxItems and maxPages : caps on rows and on pages per area. A search with a maxPrice sends the price range to Funda, so Funda does that filtering. The living-area and bedroom limits are applied by the Actor after it has read a page, so they remove rows but do not reduce the number of pages fetched. To search two towns for larger apartments for sale, the input would look like this: { "offering" : "sale" , "areas" : [ "amsterdam" , "utrecht" ] , "objectType" : "apartment" , "minLivingAreaM2" : 60 , "minBedrooms" : 2 , "maxItems" : 30 , "maxPages" : 3 } Step 3: Run it from Python This script starts the Actor, waits for it, reads the dataset and prints two lines per listing: import os from apify_client import ApifyClient # 1. Initialise the client with your token from the environment client = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ "APIFY_API_TOKEN" ] ) # 2. Describe the search: rentals in Utrecht up to 1,500 EUR a month run_input = { "offering" : "rent" , "areas" : [ "utrecht" ] , "maxPrice" : 1500 , "maxItems" : 15 , "maxPages" : 1 , } # 3. Start the Actor and wait for it to finish run = client . actor ( "reventadata/funda-scraper" ) . call ( run_input = run_input ) if run is None or run . status != "SUCCEEDED" : status = run . status if run else "unknown" raise SystemExit ( f "Run did not succeed (status: {status})." ) # 4. Read the rows from the run's default dataset items = client . dataset ( run . default_dataset_id ) . list_items ( ) . items print ( f "Retrieved {len(items)} listings.\n" ) # 5. Print two lines per listing, with a price per square metre worked out here for item in items : street = " " . join ( part for part in ( item . get ( "street" ) , item . get ( "houseNumber" ) , item . get ( "houseNumberSuffix" ) ) if part ) price , area = item . get ( "price" ) , item . get ( "livingAreaM2" ) per_m2 = f "{price / area:.1f} EUR/m2" if price and area else "no living area" print ( f "{street}, {item.get('city')} | {price} EUR/month | {area} m2 | {per_m2}" ) print ( f " {item.get('propertyType')}, bedrooms: {item.get('bedrooms')}, energy label: {item.get('energyLabel')}" ) Fetching goes through an unblocking service, one page at a time, so keep maxPages small while you test. Step 4: Read the output The loop prints one block per listing. This is the start of its output on a capture dated 2026-11-07 (a Utrecht rental search with maxPrice 1,500, 15 rows on page 1): Koningsweg 135 E, Utrecht | 290 EUR/month | None m2 | no living area parking, bedrooms: None, energy label: unknown Hooft Graaflandstraat 2 A9, Utrecht | 1425 EUR/month | 27 m2 | 52.8 EUR/m2 apartment, bedrooms: 1, energy label: A++++ Oranje Vrijbuiterslaan 55, Utrecht | 1132 EUR/month | 48 m2 | 23.6 EUR/m2 apartment, bedrooms: 1, energy label: A The first listing is a parking space: no living area, no bedrooms. The Actor keeps it because objectType was left empty, and it reports the missing values as null rather than guessing. Step 5: Add coordinates and the description (optional) Set includeDetails to true and the Actor opens each kept listing's own page for latitude, longitude, the full Dutch description and the feature table. A listing whose page cannot be read still ships, with those four fields null . The detail fields look like this on a capture of one rental listing's page (description and features shortened): { "latitude" : 52.074806 , "longitude" : 5.119643 , "description" : "Karakteristiek appartement met patio en uitzicht over de Vaartsche Rijn! ..." , "features" : { "Aangeboden sinds" : "November 6, 2026" , "Huurprijs" : "€ 1.950 per maand (geen servicekosten)" , "Waarborgsom" : "€ 3.900 eenmalig" , "Soort bouw" : "Bestaande bouw" , "Bouwjaar" : "1920" , "Wonen" : "85 m²" , "Aantal kamers" : "2 kamers (1 slaapkamer)" , "Verwarming" : "Gehele vloerverwarming" } } Understanding your results Every row carries 38 fields. The ones you will use most: price , priceCondition , priceType : the amount, and how Funda labels it ( per_month for rent, kosten_koper for sale). street , houseNumber , houseNumberSuffix , postalCode , city , district , neighbourhood : the address, split up. livingAreaM2 , plotAreaM2 , rooms , bedrooms , energyLabel : size and energy label, as published. An unlabelled home shows "unknown" . agencyName , agencyUrl , agencyAssociation , brokerName : the listing agency, and the broker when the listing names one. imageUrls , publishedAt , openHouses , promoText : photos, publication time, open-house windows, promo line. One complete row from the same capture ( imageUrls cut to its first entry): { "id" : "8178650" , "url" : "https://www.funda.nl/detail/huur/utrecht/appartement-hooft-graaflandstraat-2-a9/80987659/" , "listingType" : "rent" , "price" : 1425 , "priceType" : "regular" , "priceCondition" : "per_month" , "currency" : "EUR" , "propertyType" : "apartment" , "constructionType" : "resale" , "status" : "none" , "street" : "Hooft Graaflandstraat" , "houseNumber" : "2" , "houseNumberSuffix" : "A9" , "postalCode" : "3525VV" , "city" : "Utrecht" , "municipality" : "Utrecht" , "province" : "Utrecht" , "district" : "Wijk 07 Zuid" , "neighbourhood" : "Nieuw Hoograven-Zuid" , "livingAreaM2" : 27 , "plotAreaM2" : null , "rooms" : 2 , "bedrooms" : 1 , "energyLabel" : "A++++" , "publishedAt" : "2026-10-05T15:49:58.8659613+02:00" , "promoText" : null , "imageUrls" : [ "https://cloud.funda.nl/tiara-media/64c806c0-d856-4ab7-be06-c84e811130e4/875e471e-0738-4a5c-bcf2-6d1f795314f4" ] , "agencyName" : "Otten en Stok Makelaars" , "agencyUrl" : "https://www.funda.nl/makelaar/63878-otten-en-stok-makelaars/" , "agencyId" : 63878 , "agencyAssociation" : "VN" , "brokerName" : null , "openHouses" : [ ] , "searchUrl" : "https://www.funda.nl/zoeken/huur?selected_area=%5B%22utrecht%22%5D&price=%220-1500%22&search_result=1" , "latitude" : null , "longitude" : null , "description" : null , "features" : null } The last four fields are null without details. Pro tips Filter by type early. In that capture 5 of 15 rows were parking spaces or storage. Set objectType to apartment or house to leave them out. Use newest for monitoring. sort: "newest" puts fresh listings first, which suits a schedule that checks for new homes. minPrice alone filters after the fetch. It is only sent to Funda together with maxPrice , so by itself it removes rows but does not save pages. Add includeDetails only when you need it. See Step 5: it costs one extra request per row. Compute your own ratios. There is no price-per-square-metre field. Divide price by livingAreaM2 yourself, as the script does, and skip rows where either is null . Mind the ceiling. Funda serves at most 666 pages of 15 results (9,990) for any one search. If a search is larger, the run logs a warning; narrow it with a price range, a type or a smaller area. Troubleshooting Zero rows, status SUCCEEDED. The site answered but nothing matched, or the area slug is unknown. The status message says so. Check the spelling against a funda.nl URL. Zero rows, status FAILED. A malformed slug or a maxPrice below minPrice ends the run with a message to fix the input. Pages that could not be read also fail a run that saved nothing. Fewer rows than expected. The log ends with Skipped N: reason lines for rows removed by your limits, and Pushed N row(s). . Read it with client.log(run.id).get() . Funda's terms of use restrict automated collection, so check that your use of the data complies with them and with data-protection law. Next steps For current pricing and details, see the Store page . To repeat a search, save it as an Apify task and attach a schedule , which runs an Actor or task on a cron expression. Datasets export as JSON, CSV, XML, Excel, HTML table, RSS or JSONL ( dataset docs ), and a webhook can call your own endpoint when a run finishes ( webhook docs ). What are you planning to search for on Funda? Drop a comment! 💬 About the author: reventadata builds and publishes data extraction Actors on the Apify Store.

title: How to write a delivery and returns page Indian shoppers trust
author: krishna kumar
summary: A delivery and returns page is most useful when it answers the awkward questions before checkout: where do you deliver, when should a customer expect an update, what if a parcel arrives damaged, and how does a return actually start? For a small Indian business, accuracy matters more than impressive-sounding promises. Write the page from the steps your team can consistently follow. Separate processing from delivery Explain the difference between the time your team needs to prepare an order and the carrier’s transit time. State which locations you currently serve and how a shopper can check whether their PIN code is included. If delivery times vary by product, destination or courier, say so and describe how the estimate is shown before payment. Do not call an estimate a guarantee unless your business can honour it. Be precise about charges. Show whether delivery fees are calculated at checkout, vary by location or depend on order size, and identify any conditions that affect them. Mention how tracking is shared and what a customer should do if an update has not appeared. If the business sometimes ships in multiple parcels, explain that one order can have more than one tracking update. Keep the information consistent across product pages, checkout, confirmation messages and the policy page. Make the return rules easy to scan Use headings or a small table to explain which products are eligible, the allowed time window, the condition required, and who pays for return shipping. If a product is made to order, perishable, customised or otherwise treated differently, describe that only when it reflects your actual policy and applicable requirements. Avoid blanket wording such as “no returns under any circumstances” without checking the rules that apply to your business. Spell out the steps: how to contact support, what order information is needed, whether the customer should wait for approval before sending anything, and how to package an item. For a parcel that arrives damaged or incorrect, tell the customer how soon to notify you and what evidence helps your team investigate. Ask only for information needed to resolve the issue; do not request passwords or payment-card details. Explain what happens next Tell shoppers how you confirm a request, how they can check its status, and what happens after a return is accepted. Distinguish the inspection step from the refund or replacement step. If the refund goes through the original payment method, bank processing time may vary; state your own processing step separately rather than promising a date you cannot control. Give a monitored support channel and a realistic response window only if staff can meet it. Before publishing, ask someone outside the business to find the delivery estimate and start a sample return from a phone. Check that every promise matches your actual order workflow, then review the page whenever your delivery area or process changes. If you are commissioning a new store or revising its policy pages, compare website building companies in India against the same written scope for checkout, policy content and ongoing updates. Do not hand over policy wording without checking it against your real operations and current requirements. Disclosure: I work with MGTech Labs. This is practical writing guidance, not legal advice; confirm the policy against the rules that apply to your business.

title: Planning a website for a tiles, sanitaryware or building materials dealer
author: krishna kumar
summary: A dealer’s website should help a customer answer three practical questions before making a trip: do you handle the kind of material I need, what information should I bring, and how do I reach the right person? For tiles, sanitaryware and building materials, a clear catalogue and contact path are often more useful than a complicated storefront. Start with the questions customers ask Write down the questions staff hear in the showroom or over the phone. They might ask about tile size, finish, colour variation, bathroom fittings, cement or other product categories, delivery coverage, or what to measure before visiting. Use only categories that match your actual stock and service. The list becomes a simple plan for the site: category pages, useful buying notes, and a visible enquiry or visit option. Avoid promising live availability unless someone can keep it accurate. If stock changes frequently, say that customers should confirm availability and batch details before travelling. For products where shade or batch consistency matters, explain that customers should check requirements with the dealer and inspect samples where appropriate. Clear limitations prevent misunderstandings better than vague claims. Make the catalogue useful on a phone Organise products by the terms buyers use, not internal shorthand. On each product or category page, include the details you can verify—such as dimensions, finish, material, intended use, brand or model where relevant, and care instructions. Keep units consistent and explain abbreviations. Add a note when information varies by variant or needs confirmation. Use real, representative photos and label them honestly. A screen cannot reliably communicate exact colour, texture or shade, so tell visitors when an image is illustrative and encourage them to check a sample. Compress images so pages remain usable on mobile connections, and make the phone number, location and opening hours easy to find without scrolling through a long description. Turn browsing into a useful visit or enquiry Give visitors a short way to ask about a product: item or category, preferred contact method, and optional context such as quantity or project stage. Do not require sensitive details. Explain whether a request is for a callback, a quote, or confirmation of availability; do not imply that a message reserves stock unless your process actually does that. If customers visit in person, provide a map link and practical directions or parking information only when you can verify them. Choose a build plan you can maintain Before hiring, write a one-page scope: catalogue size, who will add or update products, whether payments are needed, who provides photography and copy, and what should happen when an item is unavailable. Ask each provider to price and demonstrate the same scope, then clarify domain ownership, administrator access, backups, training and ongoing support in writing. A web development firm in India can be assessed with those same questions; compare the answers rather than relying on a broad promise. For context, MGTech Labs is one example of a provider site to review, not a substitute for checking fit and references. Before launch, ask someone unfamiliar with the project to find a product category, locate the shop, and send an enquiry on a phone. Fix any step that makes them guess. A small, accurate catalogue that staff can keep current is a better starting point than a large collection of stale listings. Disclosure: I work with MGTech Labs. Please compare providers against your own written requirements.

title: What Is a Rage Click? 7 Causes, Dead Clicks and Fixes
author: Hamdi Bk
summary: We build Opti-Behavior, the WordPress plugin discussed here. Originally published on optiuser.com. A rage click is when a visitor clicks the same spot several times in a very short time, usually 3 or more clicks within about one second. Rage clicking almost always means the visitor expected something to happen, and it did not. Think of an elevator button you press again and again: that is exactly what rage clicks are, but on a website. A dead click is the quiet version: a single click on something that looks clickable and does nothing. Rage clicks are one of the clearest signs of a frustrated visitor. And frustrated visitors do not buy, sign up or come back. The good news: rage clicks are easy to find and often easy to fix. Simple definition: A rage click is 3 or more quick clicks on the same small area, usually within about one second. A dead click is a single click that does nothing at all. In Opti-Behavior, rage, dead and error click detection is a Pro feature; the free plugin gives you click heatmaps, where dead clicks show up as hot spots on things that are not links. Rage clicks vs dead clicks vs error clicks These three often come together. Here is the difference. Type What happens What the visitor feels Rage click Many fast clicks on the same spot "Why is this not working?!" Dead click One click, nothing changes on the page "Hmm, I thought that was a button." Error click A click that triggers a JavaScript error Often nothing visible, the feature is broken A dead click can turn into a rage click. The visitor clicks once, nothing happens, so they click again, harder. What causes rage clicks? Here are the most common causes we see on WordPress sites. Things that look clickable but are not. A product image, an icon, bold blue text, a card. People expect a link. Slow buttons. The button works, but it takes two seconds to react. The visitor clicks again because they think it failed. Broken JavaScript. A plugin conflict or an error stops a menu, a slider or an "Add to cart" button from working. On a shop, a broken checkout script is a common reason behind an abandoned cart. Tiny tap targets on mobile. The link is too small, so the finger misses it again and again. Form buttons that do not give feedback. The visitor presses "Send", nothing shows, so they press again. Pop-ups that will not close. The close button is too small or covered. Disabled buttons with no explanation. The button is grey because a field is missing, but nothing tells the visitor. How to find rage clicks on your WordPress site Option 1: Watch recordings (slow) You can open session recordings one by one and look for fast clicks. It works, but it takes hours on a busy site. Option 2: Let a tool flag them (fast) Opti-Behavior Pro detects friction events on its own. It flags rage clicks, dead clicks and error clicks, groups them by page and element, and links each one to the recording where it happened. Each line is one element where visitors got stuck, with the number of events. Open an event to see the page, the element and the recording. This turns hours of watching into a short to-do list, for example: "The 'Size guide' link on product pages gets the most rage clicks." Now you know exactly what to fix. Option 3: Check your click heatmap A click heatmap shows hot spots on things that are not links. That is where dead clicks live. It is included in the free version of Opti-Behavior. Hot spots on images or plain text often mean dead clicks. Dead clicks: the quiet cousin of rage clicks A rage click is loud. Someone hits the same spot five times in a second. A dead click is quiet. Someone clicks once on something that looks clickable, nothing happens, and they just leave. No drama, no noise. That is why dead clicks are easy to miss, and why they often cost more. Here is a typical example. Imagine a shop with a "Size guide" line under the price, in blue and underlined. It looks exactly like a link, but it is plain text. Visitors click it and nothing opens. Some of them never add to cart, because they are not sure which size to pick. Why a click can be "dead" When Opti-Behavior Pro records a dead click, it also saves the details: the element that was clicked, whether it was really interactive, whether something was covering it, what happened after the click, and the screen size, browser and device. The button "View element on page" highlights the element on your live page, so you see exactly what visitors saw. Most dead clicks come from one of these three causes: Covered by an overlay. A pop-up, a cookie banner or a sticky bar sits on top of the button. The visitor sees the button but clicks the invisible layer above it. This is very common on mobile. Not interactive. The element looks like a link or a button (blue, underlined, an arrow, a card with a shadow) but it is just text or an image. A script problem. The button should work, but its JavaScript failed to load or crashed. The verdict tells you who should fix it In Opti-Behavior Pro, each group of friction events gets a verdict, so you know if it is a design job or a developer job: Verdict What it means Who fixes it Probable code bug Clicks on this element triggered a captured error Developer Needs review Could be a bug or the network (ad blockers, offline) Check a few recordings first Visitor behavior Normal behavior, like impatient clicking Usually nobody, or a small design tweak With Pro, Smart Insights measures rage clicks per 100 visits, so a busy page does not flood you with cards. You see the elements that frustrate a real share of visitors, not every single double-click. How to fix dead clicks Covered by overlay: move or shrink the pop-up, cookie banner or sticky bar, or delay it until the visitor scrolls. Not interactive: make it a real link, or change its look so it does not pretend to be one. No blue underline on plain text. Probable code bug: open the linked JavaScript error and fix or replace the script that breaks. After the fix, check the same element two weeks later. Dead clicks on it should drop close to zero. How to fix rage clicks Fix the cause, not the symptom. Here is a simple guide. Cause Fix Image or icon looks clickable Make it a link, or change the style so it does not look clickable Button is slow Show a loading state right away ("Adding…") so people know it worked JavaScript error Check the error log, update or replace the plugin that breaks Tiny mobile link Make tap targets at least 44 by 44 pixels Form button gives no feedback Show a message or spinner right after the click Pop-up close button hard to hit Make it bigger and let people close it by tapping outside Disabled button Tell people what is missing, next to the button Measure before and after Before you fix anything, look at the verdict. Opti-Behavior Pro tells you if the clicks look like a design problem (people click something that is not a button) or a code bug (the clicks trigger an error). After a fix, compare the number of rage clicks on that element for the next two weeks. If it drops, you fixed it. If you want to be sure the change also helped sales or sign-ups, run an A/B test. Opti-Behavior's A/B testing is free. Are rage clicks always bad? Almost always, but not every time. Some people double-click out of habit. A game or a quiz may need fast clicks. That is why good tools look for a pattern: many visitors, same element, again and again. One person with a fast finger is not a problem. Fifty people on the same button is. Slow buttons and rage clicks often go together. If your page reacts slowly to taps, Core Web Vitals (especially INP) are worth a look. Rage clicks FAQ What are rage clicks? Rage clicks are several fast clicks on the same spot, usually within about one second. They show that a visitor expected something to happen and it did not. What is the difference between rage clicks and dead clicks? A dead click is one click that does nothing. A rage click is many fast clicks in the same place. A dead click often becomes a rage click when the visitor tries again. How do I track rage clicks in WordPress? Use a behavior analytics plugin that detects friction events. Opti-Behavior Pro flags rage clicks, dead clicks and error clicks and links each one to a session recording. Do rage clicks hurt conversions? They can. A rage click means a visitor tried to do something and could not, so it often marks a step where people give up. Fix the elements with the most rage clicks first, then check the effect with an A/B test. title: Making PDFs tamper-evident in the browser with SHA-256 (and why we hash the sealed file, not the original)
author: trampto
summary: AI has made it trivial to edit an invoice, a quote or a contract so cleanly that nobody can spot the change by eye. A PDF has no memory: the file name, the date and the layout all look the same after someone changes "1,800 €" to "4,800 €". So instead of trying to detect a forgery by how it looks, we built TRAMPTO to prove that a document hasn't changed, with plain math. This post walks through how it works, the one design decision that bit us, and what this approach does not prove. The idea in one line Compute a SHA-256 fingerprint of the document, register it, and give the recipient a link where they can recompute it themselves. Change one byte and the fingerprint no longer matches. Hashing in the browser with Web Crypto No libraries needed. The whole thing runs client-side with the Web Crypto API: export async function sha256Hex ( bytes : Uint8Array ) : Promise < string > { // Copy only this view's bytes: a Uint8Array can be a window // into a larger ArrayBuffer, and hashing the whole buffer // would give you a different (wrong) fingerprint. const buffer = bytes . buffer . slice ( bytes . byteOffset , bytes . byteOffset + bytes . byteLength ) as ArrayBuffer ; const digest = await crypto . subtle . digest ( "SHA-256" , buffer ) ; return Array . from ( new Uint8Array ( digest ) ) . map ( ( b ) => b . toString ( 16 ) . padStart ( 2 , "0" ) ) . join ( "" ) ; } That slice(byteOffset, …) line looks redundant until it isn't. If the bytes come from a parser or a file reader that hands you a view over a bigger buffer, hashing bytes.buffer directly silently fingerprints the wrong data. Two codebases that both "compute SHA-256 of the file" will then disagree, and every verification fails. Because the hash is computed on the device, the document itself never leaves the browser . Only the fingerprint, the file name and a seal ID go to the register. Sealing: two hashes, not one When a document is sealed, we compute two fingerprints: contentHash : SHA-256 of the original file, before we touch it. We add a tiny visual micro-seal to each page (about 6 mm, 15% opacity, bottom-right corner, respecting page rotation) and write contentHash into the PDF metadata. stampedHash : SHA-256 of the final sealed PDF . const contentHash = await sha256Hex ( pdfBytes ) ; // original const pdfDoc = await PDFDocument . load ( pdfBytes ) ; for ( const page of pdfDoc . getPages ( ) ) drawDiscreetMark ( page ) ; pdfDoc . setSubject ( `TRAMPTO-HASH:${contentHash}` ) ; const sealedBytes = new Uint8Array ( await pdfDoc . save ( ) ) ; const stampedHash = await sha256Hex ( sealedBytes ) ; // public fingerprint The public verification link is /v/{stampedHash} . The decision that matters: hash the sealed file It's tempting to make the public fingerprint the hash of the original. Don't. The file people actually send around is the sealed one. If the link pointed at the original's hash, a recipient holding the sealed PDF could never reproduce it. The order is an invariant: hash original → seal → hash sealed . If you ever change the order, the seal drawing, or touch the PDF after computing stampedHash , every link you've already issued stops verifying. We treat that sequence like a database migration: it doesn't change casually. Verifying The recipient opens the link (or drops the file on the verify page). The browser recomputes SHA-256 of the file they have and looks it up in the register: Match → the file is byte-for-byte the one that was sealed, and we show when it was sealed. No match → something changed, even a single byte. One detail worth copying: distinguish "not found" from "network error" . If the backend is down, we must not tell someone their genuine document is fake. A failed lookup throws and asks to retry; only a clean "no row" means "not verified". Other formats Word, PowerPoint, images and text are converted to PDF in the browser first (heavy libraries like pdf-lib and mammoth are loaded on demand with dynamic import() so the app opens instantly). Then the same sealing flow runs. What this does not prove Being honest about limits matters more than the feature list: It proves integrity, not authorship. It shows the file hasn't changed since it was sealed. It doesn't prove who wrote it or that its content is true. It's not a qualified e-signature. It doesn't replace eIDAS qualified signatures or seals where the law requires them. The "when" relies on our register. The sealing date comes from TRAMPTO's database, not from a blockchain or a qualified timestamp authority. For quotes, contracts, invoices, reports and certificates, where the risk is "someone quietly changed the numbers", that's usually exactly the guarantee you need. Try it trampto.com : verifying is always free, and the first 3 seals are free. I'd love feedback from other devs, especially on the verification UX for people who have never heard of a hash.

title: Context Mode Saved Me 40K Tokens Per Request (And Caught Silent Test Failures)
author: Marcus Reed
summary: The Problem Nobody Talks About Last month I spent two hours debugging why Cursor kept suggesting a deprecated API—one I'd removed three commits ago. The file was gone. Git history was clean. Yet the AI insisted the old implementation was still valid. Turns out? Context window compression had silently dropped my recent changes. The model was working with a 6-hour-old snapshot of the codebase. Why Context Compression Breaks Silently Cursor (and most AI coding tools) aggressively compress context to fit models' token limits. When your codebase crosses that threshold: Recent file changes get deprioritized Test files disappear from context entirely The AI hallucinates based on stale architecture The worst part? No warnings. You just get confident, wrong answers. Enter Context Mode I found mksglu/context-mode after the third time I shipped a bug because Cursor's context and my actual codebase had diverged. It's a dead-simple VSCode extension that shows you exactly what files are in your AI's context window —in real time, with token counts. What It Actually Does # Install code --install-extension mksglu.context-mode # Then open Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P) # Search: "Context Mode: Show Active Context" You get a live panel showing: Which files are currently loaded (by priority) Token count per file What got dropped due to limits Real-World Impact Before Context Mode: Me: "Why is the login test failing?" Cursor: "The test passes locally for me." [30 min of confusion] Turns out: test file wasn't in context After Context Mode: Context panel shows : auth . test . ts ( excluded - token limit ) Me : [ adds . cursorrules to prioritize test files ] Cursor : [ actually sees the failing assertion ] My .cursorrules Setup I now force-include critical files that Cursor's auto-prioritization misses: # .cursorrules context : always_include : - "**/*.test.ts" - "**/*.spec.ts" - "vitest.config.ts" - "tsconfig.json" exclude : - "node_modules/**" - "dist/**" - "*.log" This cut my context size from 52K → 12K tokens while keeping test coverage visible. The Verification Script I added this to my pre-commit hook: #!/bin/bash # .git/hooks/pre-commit # Check if critical files are in Cursor's context context_check ( ) { local file = $1 if ! cursor-context-cli contains "$file" ; then echo "⚠️ $file missing from AI context" exit 1 fi } context_check "vitest.config.ts" context_check "src/**/*.test.ts" (Note: cursor-context-cli is a hypothetical wrapper—Context Mode doesn't ship a CLI yet, but the VSCode API makes this trivial to build.) What I Learned AI coding tools lie by omission. If a file isn't in context, the model will confidently work around its absence. Token budgets are not fungible. Dropping test files to fit more source code is almost always the wrong tradeoff. Verification is cheaper than debugging. Spending 5 seconds checking Context Mode beats spending 20 minutes chasing phantom bugs. The Dilemma I'm Still Solving Context Mode solved visibility, but I'm still wrestling with prioritization: If I force-include all tests, I hit token limits on large PRs If I let Cursor auto-prioritize, it drops the exact test that would've caught my bug Manual context curation per task feels like fighting the tool How do you decide what belongs in context when everything feels critical?

title: Setting Up a New MacBook for AI Coding in 2026: The 12 Apps I'd Install First
author: E Daugherty
summary: A fresh MacBook is the best and worst day of the year. Everything is fast, and nothing works the way your hands expect. This is the list I'd run through before writing a single line of code: the free basics first, then the AI tools, then the small utilities that make a laptop feel like yours. Every app here is real, current, and linked to its official page. The foundation 1. Homebrew Install this before anything else. Almost every app below has a brew install --cask line, so a new machine becomes one script instead of an afternoon of download pages. brew.sh 2. Ghostty A free, open-source terminal with a native macOS feel. It is fast, configured with a plain text file, and does not ask you to sign in to anything. ghostty.org 3. Raycast The launcher I'd set to Cmd+Space on day one. The free plan already covers clipboard history, window management, snippets and the community extension store. Pro adds Raycast AI and starts at $96 a year. raycast.com Window and keyboard sanity 4. Rectangle Move and resize windows with keyboard shortcuts or by dragging to screen edges. Free and open source, macOS 14+. If you used Spectacle years ago, Rectangle can start with its default shortcuts. rectangleapp.com 5. AltTab Cmd+Tab switches apps. AltTab switches windows, with previews, including minimized ones and windows on other Spaces. The core app is free and open source (GPL-3.0); Pro adds search and extra styles. alt-tab.app 6. Maccy A clipboard manager that does exactly one job. Hit the shortcut, type a few letters, press Enter. MIT licensed, free, macOS 14+, and it drops passwords your password manager clears from the clipboard. maccy.app The AI coding layer 7. Cursor An AI code editor built on the VS Code base, so your extensions and keybindings come along. Worth installing even if you live in another editor, just to compare how it handles multi-file edits. cursor.com 8. Claude Code Anthropic's coding agent that runs in your terminal. Pair it with Ghostty and a couple of tabs and you have a very capable setup with almost nothing on screen. claude.com/product/claude-code 9. Wispr Flow Voice dictation that works across your apps. Useful for long prompts to an agent, where talking through the problem is faster than typing it. There is a free plan on Mac; Pro removes the usage limits. wisprflow.ai The menu bar 10. Ice A new Mac fills the menu bar fast, and the notch eats whatever does not fit. Ice hides the icons you rarely need, can show them in a separate bar below the notch, and lets you drag items into order. Free and open source, macOS 14+. github.com/jordanbaird/Ice 11. TokenBar Once Cursor, Claude Code and Codex are all on the machine, each one has its own limits and its own reset time. TokenBar puts usage and reset times for Claude, Codex, Cursor, Gemini and Copilot in the menu bar, with a fuller dashboard when you need it. It is built on Peter Steinberger's open-source CodexBar (MIT) and includes a Pixel Agents view for seeing which coding agents are working or waiting. It does not give you extra quota; it just shows what is left. $5/month Basic or $15 lifetime Pro, macOS 14+. tokenbar.site 12. CleanShot X Screenshots, screen recordings, annotation and scrolling capture in one app. Handy for bug reports and PR descriptions. $35 one-time for the Mac app with a year of updates, or on Setapp. Requires macOS 13+. cleanshot.com The install script Most of the list in one go: brew install --cask ghostty raycast rectangle alt-tab maccy cursor jordanbaird-ice cleanshot Then grab Claude Code, Wispr Flow and TokenBar from their sites. Your turn What is the first app you install on a new Mac that nobody else seems to know about? Drop it in the comments. I'm always looking for the thirteenth item.

title: Your agent is probably running stale skills
author: Louis Esterhuizen
summary: Agent skills are folders with a SKILL.md that teach Claude Code, Codex and other agents how to do something specific: review a React app, plan a feature with Spec Kit, write a Hugging Face training script. They're easy to share, so most people install them the simple way, by copying the folder into their skills directory. That's where it goes quietly wrong. Once a skill is copied, nothing tracks it. The author fixes a mistake, adapts to a new API, or rewrites the instructions, and your copy stays as it was. And a stale skill doesn't fail. There's no error, just an agent that follows last spring's advice and does slightly worse work, and you have no reason to suspect the skill. How common is this? I counted the 597 SKILL.md files in seven of the biggest public collections: Anthropic's, OpenAI's, GitHub's awesome-copilot, Hugging Face's, Vercel's, obra/superpowers, and the skills bundled with Codex. Only 41 record a version at all ( metadata.version ), and only 17 say where they came from ( metadata.source ). Most of those versions are "1.0" or "1.0.0" , and they stay that way. Vercel's react-best-practices has changed in more than ten commits since January and still says 1.0.0 . So even when a skill has a version number, comparing version numbers would miss most updates. And 580 of the 597 carry no record of where they came from, so a copy of one can't find its way back. What I built skill-check is a small open-source plugin for Claude Code and Codex. At the moment a skill is used, it checks whether a newer version exists and, if so, shows a warning: [skill-check] The skill "speckit-plan" is out of date: installed 0.12.0, latest v0.13.1. Run `specify self upgrade`, then `specify integration upgrade claude` in this project. The agent sees the warning too, mentions it to you, and carries on. Nothing is blocked. It knows a skill is stale in three ways: metadata.source in the SKILL.md. It compares your copy with the upstream copy at that URL: by version when upstream's is higher, otherwise by content and, for GitHub sources, the file's commit history. That's how it catches the 1.0.0 skill that changed ten times: it matches your copy to the commit it came from and sees that upstream has moved on. Spec Kit. speckit-* skills are compared with the latest Spec Kit release. npx skills . Skills installed with npx skills add are compared with the hash in its lock file. A check runs in the background when a session starts, and results are cached for a day, so using a skill is instant. Offline or rate-limited means silence, never a broken session. It has no server and no telemetry, and it only fetches the public files it compares against. The convention matters more than the tool The part I care about most is two lines any skill author can add today, with no changes to the Agent Skills spec: metadata : version : 1.2.0 source : https://github.com/you/your-skills/tree/main/your-skill source is the important one: it travels with every copy, so any tool, not just mine, can find the upstream again. version is a useful hint on top. I've written it up as a short convention ( CONVENTION.md , CC BY 4.0) and shared the evidence on the Agent Skills spec discussion that proposes the same keys. If agents end up checking this natively, skill-check will have done its job. Try it Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add louis8408/skill-check /plugin install skill-check@skill-check Codex: codex plugin marketplace add louis8408/skill-check codex plugin add skill-check@skill-check You need Node.js 20 or later. The README has a two-minute "Try it" that installs an outdated example skill so you can see the warning, and a check command that lists the status of every skill you have. If you maintain skills: please add metadata.source . It's one line, and it's what lets your fixes reach the people who copied your skill. I built skill-check with Claude Code's help, and Claude Code helped draft this post.
